{"filepath":"comparison_report.md","content":"# Comparison Report: Residential LFP (LiFePO4) vs Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries (VRFB)

Prepared: 10 September 2026
Sources: lfp_battery_research.md, vanadium_flow_battery_research.md, team_discussion.md (see References)

Purpose
- Consolidate team research and meeting outcomes into a single, actionable comparison for homeowners, integrators, and local planners considering LFP (LiFePO4) and VRFB (vanadium redox flow) systems for residential use.

Executive summary & recommendation
- Recommendation (short): For most single‑household residential use cases (daily solar self‑consumption, backup for overnight outages, compact installs), LFP (LiFePO4) is the recommended default: it is mature, compact, higher round‑trip efficiency, broadly available, and generally lower installed cost per usable kWh today. For explicit long‑duration resilience (multi‑day backup, >6–12+ hours of stored energy) or very high cycle/throughput requirements, VRFBs are compelling where site space, maintenance, and higher up‑front cost are acceptable.

- Best use cases (at a glance):
  - LFP: daily solar shifting & peak‑shaving, typical home backup (hours), retrofit installs, constrained footprint, customers prioritising low O&M and broad installer ecosystem.
  - VRFB: long‑duration resilience (6+ to 24+ hours), sites expecting very high cycle counts (frequent deep cycling), deployments where non‑flammability and long calendar life are top priorities, and community/microgrid installations where decoupled power/energy scaling is valuable.

Side‑by‑side comparison (system‑level, usable‑kWh normalised)
- Notes on normalization: all metrics below are system‑level and expressed on a usable‑kWh basis where meaningful. Cycle life is expressed as cycles to ~80% of initial usable capacity at the stated DoD. Ranges reflect vendor datasheets, independent reports and market studies; where the team flagged numbers as inconsistent or materially uncertain, they are marked as [UNCERTAIN] with explanation in the Detailed sections and the Open Questions section.

| Metric (system level, usable‑kWh basis) | LFP (LiFePO4) | VRFB (Vanadium flow) | Comment / Confidence |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Typical system round‑trip efficiency (RTE) | 90% – 96% | 65% – 80% **[UNCERTAIN]** | LFP: well‑established high RTE at inverter/system level. VRFB: vendor/lab ranges vary; 70–80% typical in many sources but can be lower at high power or low temp. See "RTE" in Detailed sections. |
| Usable DoD (practical) | 80% – 100% usable | 80% – 100% usable | Both can be operated deep; LFP vendors often limit DoD in warranty terms. Confidence: high. |
| Cycle life (to ~80% @ typical DoD) | 3,000 – 10,000+ cycles (depends on DoD) **[UNCERTAIN RANGE]** | >10,000 – 25,000+ cycles (vendor claims) | LFP cycle life varies widely by vendor and DoD; VRFB vendors claim very high cycle counts but require ongoing maintenance. See notes below. |
| Calendar / design life | 10 – 20 years (typical warranties 10 yrs) | 15 – 30 years (vendor projections) | VRFB calendar life projections are optimistic but depend on O&M. |
| Installed cost ($/usable kWh) | **$800 – $2,000 / kWh** (system installed) **[UNCERTAIN]** | **$1,000 – $2,500+ / kWh** (small/residential installs) **[UNCERTAIN]** | Large variation by region, incentives, vendor. VRFB small‑scale installed costs carry a premium. (See Cost section.) |
| Footprint / weight | Compact (lowest footprint per kWh) | Larger footprint (tanks, pumps, stack) | Important for constrained yards/garages. |
| Safety (fire risk) | Moderate (battery fire risk; LFP is lower risk vs other Li chemistries) | Low (aqueous, non‑flammable electrolyte) | VRFB advantage for fire‑sensitive installations. |
| O&M & maintenance | Low (BMS updates, occasional checks) | Higher (pumps, electrolyte checks, containment) | VRFB requires periodic maintenance and potential electrolyte handling. |
| Typical minimum practical system size | 5 – 20 kWh retail modules common | Few off‑the‑shelf <100 kWh modules; residential adaptation often 100s kWh | VRFB availability at small residential scale is limited; retrofit feasibility constrained. **[UNCERTAIN: minimum viable residential size varies by vendor]** |
| Typical vendors (examples) | BYD, Pylontech, LG Energy (LFP lines), many integrators | Invinity, Rongke, Sumitomo, smaller specialist vendors | Market focus differs: LFP many consumer vendors; VRFB mostly C&I / grid vendors. |

Detailed summaries

LFP (Lithium Iron Phosphate) — detailed summary
- What it is: LFP (LiFePO4) is a lithium‑ion cathode chemistry prioritising safety and longevity over maximum energy density. In residential systems LFP cells are packaged into modules/packs with an integrated BMS, thermal management and often an inverter (AC‑coupled) or DC‑coupled architecture.

- Performance highlights:
  - System round‑trip efficiency: commonly 90–96% at the system level (including inverter losses). This high efficiency improves daily arbitrage economics for self‑consumption.
  - Usable DoD: many LFP packs allow 80–100% usable capacity; vendors commonly recommend ~80–95% to balance warranty and life.
  - Cycle life: published ranges vary. Typical marketing and datasheet figures: 3,000–6,000 cycles at deep DoD for many residential packs; some vendor‑lab claims exceed 10,000 cycles under controlled conditions. Cycle life is highly dependent on DoD, average SOC, temperature and charge/discharge rates. Because of variance across datasheets, the team marked published upper bounds as **[UNCERTAIN RANGE]** and recommends vendor‑specific validation for procurement.
  - Calendar life / warranty: typical product warranties 10 years (some vendors offer 10–15 years or throughput based warranties). Expected calendar life for well‑operated packs is ~10–20 years, though replacement earlier is possible depending on duty cycle.

- Safety & thermal management:
  - LFP has a favorable thermal profile compared to NMC/NCA chemistries — lower thermal runaway risk — but still requires proper enclosure, ventilation and compliant installation (UL 9540, local codes). BMS functions (cell balancing, temperature monitoring) are essential.

- Cost & procurement notes:
  - Installed cost ranges are wide: team sources aggregated conservative installed cost estimates at roughly $800–$2,000 per kWh installed (system level) depending on region, inverter selection, incentives and installer labour. This range was explicitly discussed in the meeting and flagged as **[UNCERTAIN]** due to market variation and timing of quotes. For procurement, request itemised quotes on a usable‑kWh basis (include BOS & inverter) — action item noted in team meeting.

- Pros & cons (quick):
  - Pros: Mature, high RTE, compact, widely supported by installers, good safety profile for Li family, good middle‑of‑road cost.
  - Cons: Finite cycle life relative to VRFB claims, fire risk (lower than many Li chemistries but present), recycling infrastructure and second‑life pathways evolving.

- Practical sizing guidance for a 3–6 kW PV household (rule‑of‑thumb):
  - Self‑consumption focus: 5–10 kWh usable for modest shifting; 10–15 kWh for larger daytime export capture.
  - Backup focus (single night): 5–12 kWh depending on critical loads; include inverter routing and automatic transfer switch requirements.
  - The team advises customised sizing with load profiles and resilience goals; see "Recommended decision criteria" section.

Vanadium Redox Flow Battery (VRFB) — detailed summary
- What it is: VRFB stores energy in vanadium ions dissolved in aqueous sulfuric (or mixed) electrolyte. Energy capacity is determined by electrolyte volume (tanks); power by the size/number of stacks. This decoupling enables flexible duration sizing.

- Performance highlights:
  - System round‑trip efficiency (RTE): literature and vendor collateral report a broad range, commonly 70–80% in many commercial systems; some reports indicate 65–85% depending on stack design, pumping losses and operating conditions. Because vendor and lab values differ materially, the team labelled the VRFB RTE range as **[UNCERTAIN]** in the comparison table and recommends system‑level test/quote verification for procurement.
  - Usable DoD: effectively 100% electrochemically; practical control strategies often operate 80–100% usable. This is an advantage for long‑duration and deep‑discharge use.
  - Cycle life: vendors and lab sources commonly claim >10,000 cycles, with some claims in the 12,000–25,000+ cycle range. These high cycle numbers reflect the chemistry’s resilience; the team treats vendor upper bounds as optimistic until corroborated by independent long‑term field data. Life is also conditional on regular O&M (membrane health, pump servicing, electrolyte integrity).
  - Calendar life / design life: vendor projections often 15–30 years with appropriate maintenance. Long calendar life is a key VRFB selling point versus Li‑ion.

- Safety & maintenance:
  - Safety: aqueous non‑flammable electrolyte yields much lower fire risk than Li‑ion; that is materially advantageous for installations with stringent fire or insurance constraints.
  - Maintenance: requires periodic O&M (pump servicing, electrolyte monitoring, containment checks). Electrolyte handling requires spill containment and PPE. Freeze protection may be needed in cold climates.

- Cost & procurement notes:
  - Cost ranges are wide and scale‑sensitive. Published mid‑2020s numbers show standalone capital costs for large deployments in the low‑hundreds $/kWh (at scale) but small/residential installations are much costlier per kWh. The team aggregated plausible installed costs for small/residential VRFBs at **$1,000–$2,500+/kWh** (system installed), and flagged this as **[UNCERTAIN]** — the uncertainty primarily stems from limited vendor pricing at residential scales, minimum module sizes, and vanadium raw material price volatility. For procurement, require itemised installed quotes and minimal system sizes from vendors (action items recorded in the meeting).

- Practical considerations and minimum sizes:
  - Few vendors offer off‑the‑shelf 10–20 kWh residential VRFB products; common module sizes in the market today are 100s of kWh and up. Adapting a VRFB for a single home is therefore often either: (a) oversized for the homeowner, or (b) available only through custom engineering and higher per‑kWh cost. Team flagged the minimum viable residential size as **[UNCERTAIN]** and an action item for vendor quotes was assigned.

- Pros & cons (quick):
  - Pros: Long calendar life, very high cycle life claims, non‑flammable, flexible energy scaling for long durations.
  - Cons: Lower system efficiency (RTE), larger footprint, higher O&M and site complexity, limited small‑scale product availability and higher installed cost per usable kWh today.

Discussion of tradeoffs (cost, lifespan, efficiency, safety, installation)
- Cost (installed $/usable kWh):
  - LFP: aggregated range ~ $800 – $2,000 / kWh installed (system level). This range includes small installer premiums and AC vs DC coupling choices. Team marked this as **[UNCERTAIN]** because prices vary rapidly by market and incentives; action item: obtain itemised vendor quotes (Owner: Alice) due 17 Sep 2026.
  - VRFB: aggregated small/residential installed estimate ~ $1,000 – $2,500+ / kWh installed. The upper end is common when vendors need to downsize C&I modules for single‑household use. VRFB installed cost is highly scale dependent; at utility/C&I scale costs may be much lower per kWh. Confidence: low/medium; further vendor quotes needed (Owner: Bob).

- Lifespan & cycles:
  - LFP: typical 3,000–10,000+ cycles (depends on DoD and operating conditions); warranties often 10 years or throughput‑limited. The team recommends using cycles to 80% at the chosen DoD for LCOS input. Uncertainty: vendor claims vary; mark upper bounds as **[UNCERTAIN RANGE]**.
  - VRFB: vendors claim >10,000 up to 25,000+ cycles and 15–30 years calendar life with maintenance. These claims are attractive but rely on maintenance and are less represented in long‑term field datasets for residential contexts. Confidence: medium, contingent on maintenance regime. Note: electrolyte is reusable and replacement cost is material (vanadium is an ongoing asset but also a cost if electrolyte replacement or top‑up required).

- Efficiency (round‑trip efficiency):
  - LFP: high (90–96%), meaning less energy lost per cycle and better economics for daily arbitrage and frequent cycling.
  - VRFB: lower (typical vendor ranges 70–80% but some reports 65–85%); this reduces the value of energy shifted daily but is less important for rare multi‑day events where stored energy replacement cost is more valuable. Uncertainty arises from vendor vs lab test discrepancies and system‑level parasitics (pumps, inverters).

- Safety & regulatory considerations:
  - LFP: lower thermal risk among lithium chemistries but still requires fire‑safe enclosures and adherence to local codes. Insurance and permitting may still require additional mitigations in some jurisdictions.
  - VRFB: aqueous, non‑flammable electrolytes simplify fire safety concerns, can ease permitting in fire‑sensitive buildings, but introduce chemical containment, spill response and corrosion concerns.

- Installation, footprint & O&M:
  - LFP: compact wall‑mount or floor‑standing packs; generally straightforward for most residential installers; minimal routine O&M beyond monitoring and occasional firmware/BMS updates.
  - VRFB: requires tanks, pumps, piping, HVAC or freeze protection in some climates; larger footprint and higher BOS complexity. Ongoing O&M (pump servicing, electrolyte checks) is a real cost and needs to be included in procurement evaluations. Minimum install size and lead times are often longer; vendors typically focus on commercial/utility customers.

Recommended decision criteria for homeowners (actionable)
- Use case first: choose the technology that matches the primary use case.
  - Primary goal = daily solar self‑consumption / peak shaving: default to LFP unless the homeowner has very large daily energy requirements that favour flow scaling.
  - Primary goal = backup for short outages (hours to single overnight): LFP is typically the most cost‑effective and installer‑friendly.
  - Primary goal = multi‑day resilience (e.g., 24–72 hours) or frequent deep cycling with long calendar life required: consider VRFB, but only after getting dealer quotes and confirming minimum viable system size and O&M commitments.

- Size to the critical load, not just total load: for backup, calculate kWh needed for critical circuits (refrigeration, medical equipment, communications) and size battery accordingly. Smaller LFP systems are typically more cost‑effective for limited critical loads.

- Compare on usable‑kWh and lifecycle cost (LCOS) terms, not nominal nameplate:
  - Ask vendors for: usable kWh, guaranteed cycles to X% capacity at stated DoD, system‑level RTE, warranty terms (years and throughput caps), and itemised installed price including inverter/BOS.
  - Convert quotes to $/usable kWh installed and to LCOS under your expected cycles/year and discount rate.

- Verify service & warranty commitments:
  - For VRFB: get O&M schedule and estimated annual O&M costs, electrolyte management policy, and any consumables replacement schedules.
  - For LFP: confirm thermal management, recommended operating SOC window, and warranty exclusions (e.g., frequent deep cycling may void parts of warranty).

- Site & permitting checks:
  - LFP: confirm room for inverter and battery, ventilation needs, and fire‑safety plan.
  - VRFB: confirm space for tanks, secondary containment, HVAC/freeze protection, and chemical handling rules; local building code and insurance implications may differ.

- Procurement checklist for every homeowner quote:
  1) Usable kWh (DoD) and guaranteed cycles to X% capacity. 2) System RTE (system‑level). 3) Itemised installed cost ($/usable kWh) including BOS. 4) Warranty years and throughput caps. 5) O&M schedule and expected annual cost. 6) Minimum system size and lead time. 7) Installer references and sample field performance data. 8) Safety & permitting checklist completed.

Open questions and outstanding uncertainties (action items recorded in meeting)
- Key unresolved items the team agreed to pursue (owners & due dates replicated from team_discussion.md):
  1) Vendor datasheets and itemised installed quotes on a usable kWh basis for shortlisted LFP and VRFB candidate products (including BOS). Owner: Alice. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
  2) Real‑world installed system round‑trip efficiency measurements and independent test reports for candidate products (system‑level). Owner: Bob. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
  3) Warranty text, throughput caps, conditional warranty clauses, and sample O&M contract excerpts for shortlisted products. Owner: Eve. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
  4) Residential‑scale installed cost data for VRFB systems (benchmarks or vendor quotes), plus minimum viable project size for typical local installers. Owner: Bob. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
  5) Ongoing O&M cost estimates (annual) for VRFB and LFP (labor, electrolyte top‑up, maintenance visits). Owner: Eve. Deadline: 17 Sep 2026.
  6) LCOS model template and a first‑pass run using best‑available numbers and ranges (present results and sensitivity to key inputs). Owner: Boss Dave. Deadline: 24 Sep 2026.

- Numbers explicitly flagged by the team as uncertain (explainers):
  - Installed cost ranges for both chemistries (LFP: $800–$2,000 / kWh; VRFB residential: $1,000–$2,500+/kWh): wide variation driven by geography, BOS selection, incentives, and market timing. Action: require itemised quotes.
  - VRFB system RTE: vendor/lab values differ; efficiency depends on power/current, pumping losses, and thermal control strategy (some vendors quote 70–80% while others publish optimized stack test results approaching ~80–85%). Action: request system‑level efficiency tests or guarantees.
  - Cycle life upper bounds (LFP and VRFB): vendors often publish optimistic lab figures; use cycles‑to‑80% at the selected DoD for conservative LCOS inputs.
  - Minimum practical residential VRFB size: unclear — market shows few true 10–20 kWh products. Action: vendor clarification required.

Consolidated References (selected primary sources and additional reading)
- Internal artifacts (this report draws on the three team files):
  - lfp_battery_research.md — Alice, 10 Sep 2026. (source file in project folder)
  - vanadium_flow_battery_research.md — Alice, 10 Sep 2026. (source file in project folder)
  - team_discussion.md — Meeting notes, 10 Sep 2026. (project meeting record)

- External references (representative vendor/technical sources cited in the research):
  - Invinity Energy Systems — Product and Endurium/VS3 pages. https://www.invinity.com
  - Rongke Power (RKP) VRFB product pages. https://www.rongkepower.cn (vendor site)
  - PNNL flow battery overview & reports. https://www.pnnl.gov
  - NREL / DOE stationary storage overviews. https://www.nrel.gov
  - IEA and industry market reports on battery costs and stationary storage. https://www.iea.org and https://www.bnef.com

- Notes on provenance: where the team used vendor datasheets and market reports the report includes ranges rather than single point estimates. For procurement decisions always request vendor datasheets, independent test reports and itemised installed quotes and convert to $/usable kWh and LCOS on your expected duty cycle.

Appendix — Quick checklist for vendor quote evaluation (copyable for homeowners/installs)
1) Usable kWh and stated DoD. 2) System RTE (system level). 3) Guaranteed cycles to X% at stated DoD. 4) Warranty years and throughput caps. 5) Itemised installed cost including BOS and inverter. 6) O&M schedule and annual cost estimate. 7) Minimum system size and lead time. 8) Safety certifications (UL 9540, IEC 62619, local approvals). 9) Installer references and field performance examples.

Prepared by: Alice (research synthesis) / Team (meeting inputs recorded by Boss Dave)

-- End of comparison_report.md --
